findings.title: Legacy writes inherit a request context that is cancelled after the response
findings.body: The background legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context. Once the REST handler returns, that parent context is normally cancelled, which immediately cancels the child context and can prevent the legacy Create from reaching storage. The same pattern is used by Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. This makes replication scheduler-dependent and can leave legacy permanently stale even though the unified write was reported successful. Create an independent background context (while preserving required request values such as tenant identity) and track/drain it as part of shutdown.

findings.title: Asynchronous replica writes can be applied out of order
findings.body: Each successful primary write starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource ordering or serialization. For example, a unified Create followed by a unified Delete can schedule a slow legacy Create and a fast legacy Delete; the delete runs first against an absent legacy object, then the delayed create leaves the object present in legacy after it is deleted in unified storage. Since mode 3 reads unified storage, this divergence is hidden until a legacy endpoint is used or a rollback occurs. Replica writes need a serialized queue or per-key ordering mechanism.

findings.title: Every write creates an unbounded 10-second background operation
findings.body: There is no queue, semaphore, or worker limit around the goroutine per write. If legacy storage is slow or unavailable, each incoming write can retain a goroutine, request data, and a legacy connection attempt for up to ten seconds. At normal write volume this can grow without bound and overload the API server and legacy backend. Use a bounded worker pool/queue with defined overload behavior.

findings.title: Update replays the update transform against a different store state
findings.body: The legacy Update receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo after Storage.Update has already consumed it. UpdatedObjectInfo produces an object from the current old object, so patches, applies, resource-version checks, and stateful transformers can produce a different result when invoked again against the legacy object's state. The previous implementation explicitly evaluated and wrapped the update before writing both stores; removing that behavior means mode 3 can report a successful unified update while applying different content, or a conflict, in legacy. Preserve a prepared update/result and the necessary resource-version translation when issuing the asynchronous replica write.

findings.title: A primary NotFound no longer cleans up a stale legacy object
findings.body: Delete now returns immediately for every Storage.Delete error. The prior implementation treated a unified-storage NotFound specially: it still issued Legacy.Delete while returning the primary NotFound result. If the stores have already drifted, deleting an object that is absent in unified storage now leaves the stale legacy object intact and still available through legacy paths (or after rollback). Retain the legacy cleanup attempt for primary NotFound errors.

findings.title: Successful delete metrics use an object name as the resource label
findings.body: The third argument to recordStorageDuration is the resource/kind label; every other mode-3 path passes options.Kind. This successful-delete path passes name instead, creating a distinct Prometheus time series for every deleted object and making success and failure metrics use incompatible labels. A workload deleting many unique names can cause avoidable metric-cardinality growth. Pass options.Kind here.

findings.title: Several mode-3 duration measurements are recorded against the wrong store
findings.body: When Storage.Create fails, this records a legacy duration rather than a storage duration; Update has the same error at line 129. Conversely, the asynchronous Legacy.DeleteCollection call at line 166 records a storage duration. This hides primary failures and reports legacy failures as storage failures, so dashboards and alerts cannot accurately detect replication or unified-storage health. Record each operation on its corresponding collector.

findings.title: Unit tests do not verify the asynchronous replica calls
findings.body: The tests return immediately after the primary operation and never wait for or assert the background legacy call. Moreover, ls and us wrap the same mock instance (lines 53-54), so an unconstrained expectation set up for Storage can also satisfy Legacy; no AssertExpectations call checks either call count or destination. Consequently these tests can pass if replication is delayed, omitted, or sent to the wrong store. Use separate mocks and a channel/WaitGroup or a deterministic replica executor to assert legacy execution, error handling, and timeout behavior.

findings.title: The new mode-3 integration test assumes legacy replication is synchronous
findings.body: The mode-3 subtest invokes doPlaylistTests, which immediately compares legacy API results after Kubernetes creates, updates, and deletes (for example the legacy list at line 522 and the legacy reads in getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 intentionally performs those legacy writes asynchronously, so these assertions race the replica goroutines and will be flaky with a slow legacy backend. Wait eventually for the expected legacy state, or expose a test hook to drain the replica queue before asserting it.
